prompt.context: A producer of high-end refrigerators in India has hired McKinsey to help him solve a profitability problem. Two years ago the company had a record year in terms of growth. Though they were correct in understanding the size of the market and how it would grow, their gross profit decreased by approximately 70% and the CEO is very worried about the situation.
prompt.question: The client has asked us to identify what happened and what can be done to restore profitability.

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of India?

clarifying_info.a: The interviewer is not sure — the candidate should estimate (assume 5 people per household = 160 million households).

clarifying_info.q: What kind of refrigerators does the client produce?
clarifying_info.a: The client builds and sells high-end units.

clarifying_info.q: How many units were sold in the market in recent years?
clarifying_info.a: Last year sales were 6 million units; two years ago they were 5 million units.
No. Although the client built a new plant, there is no problem on the cost side — a prior engagement streamlined all operations.

exhibits.title: Market Sizing Table
exhibits.shows: A table laying out population, households, units sold, years between refrigerator changes, and implied market size for two consecutive years
exhibits.data: Population: 800,000,000; People per household: 5; Households: 160,000,000; Units sold two years ago: 5,000,000; Units sold last year: 6,000,000; Years between change: 7; Implied market size two years ago: 35,000,000; Implied market size last year: 42,000,000

framework: Break profit into Revenue and Costs
On costs: check for new capex (new plant), depreciation, interest on debt — interviewer confirms costs are not the issue
On revenue: size the total addressable market using population → households → penetration rate → replacement cycle
Identify whether market growth is coming from a segment the client does not serve (low-end vs. high-end)
Evaluate strategic options to address the gap
Quantitatively test any proposed pricing or volume change against a break-even condition

questions.prompt: Size the Indian refrigerator market and determine how many households currently own a refrigerator.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use: 800M population ÷ 5 per household = 160M households. Multiply units sold × replacement cycle (7 years) to get implied installed base. Compare to total households to get penetration rate. Conclude that only ~26% of households own a refrigerator, signaling most growth is coming from first-time buyers in lower-income segments.

math.setup: Implied installed base = annual units sold × years between replacement. Penetration = installed base ÷ total households.
math.answer: Only ~26% of households own a refrigerator, meaning 74% of households — likely lower-income — do not yet have one. The market growth is concentrated in segments the high-end client does not competitively serve.

questions.prompt: The marketing director proposes cutting price by 20% to appeal to the lower-income segment, expecting a 30% sales increase. Should the client support this?
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up the profit inequality: new revenue must exceed new costs. Express in terms of P (price), C (COGS), Q (quantity). Solve for the break-even C/P ratio and assess whether it is realistic. A COGS/Price ratio of 80% is plausible for a manufacturer; if COGS is only ~25% of price, the price cut destroys value.

math.setup: Profit condition: new_revenue − new_cost > 0, i.e. (0.8P)(1.3Q) − C(1.3Q) > 0
steps: Interpretation: the price cut is value-neutral if COGS = 80% of price, and value-destructive if COGS < 80% of price (e.g., if COGS is only 25% of price, the move is bad)
math.answer: Break-even C/P ratio is 80%. If the client's COGS is well below 80% of price (e.g., 25%), reducing price by 20% for a 30% volume gain destroys profit and should not be supported without further data.

brainstorming.prompt: What options does the client have to restore profitability and capture growth from lower-income segments?

categories.name: Product / Capacity
ideas: Use excess capacity in the new plant to build lower-end refrigerators targeting lower-income households
Design a stripped-down product line suited to lower-income needs (smaller size, simpler features, lower price point)

categories.name: Branding
ideas: Launch the lower-end line under a separate sub-brand to protect the premium brand equity
Use a flanker brand strategy so the high-end line is not diluted

categories.name: Distribution / Financing
ideas: Offer consumer financing or installment plans to make high-end or mid-tier units accessible to lower-income buyers
Partner with microfinance institutions or banks to extend credit

categories.name: Geographic Expansion
ideas: Export excess production capacity to other markets where the high-end product is competitive
Target other emerging markets with similar growth dynamics

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Avoid a blanket price cut on the existing product; instead introduce a separately priced entry-level SKU
Consider value-added bundles (warranty, service) to justify premium pricing in existing segments

recommendation: The client's profitability decline is driven by a revenue mix problem: the Indian refrigerator market is growing primarily through lower-income first-time buyers (only 26% penetration), a segment the high-end client does not competitively address
The recommended path is to leverage spare capacity in the new plant to launch a lower-end or mid-tier product line under a separate brand, capturing growth without eroding the premium brand
risks: Brand dilution if the lower-end line is not clearly separated from the premium offering
Operational complexity from managing two product tiers with different cost structures
A blanket 20% price cut on the existing product is likely value-destructive unless COGS/Price exceeds 80%
next_steps: Conduct consumer research to define price points and feature requirements for the lower-income segment
Assess plant capacity and incremental unit economics for a lower-end SKU
Design a flanker brand strategy and go-to-market plan
Evaluate financing partnerships to reduce affordability barriers
